title: The world's creation is false
hook: jag rachnaa sabh jhooth hai: know, friend, that this created world is passing (Salok M9, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam, and your line: the name is the boat. Did you say the Name, or one steady word, when worry pulled? Today is day six hundred, and the salok we reach uses a word that's easy to misunderstand. Day six hundred.

When a friend tells you a promise is false, you know what they mean: it was a lie. Someone set out to fool you. So if you open an English translation of today's salok and read that the world's creation is false, it sounds startling. Is the scripture saying the sunrise is a lie? Your grandmother's hands? The bread on the table? That's not how Sikhs hear it. The key is in the second half of the couplet, and in a picture anyone who has played with dry sand knows: pile it into a wall, and it starts slipping the moment you take your hands away.
screen: `FALSE: A LIE?` → `THE SUNRISE, THE BREAD, THE HANDS.` → `THE SECOND HALF OF THE COUPLET.`

segments.voice: The salok says jag rachnaa sabh jhooth hai, jaan lehu re meet. In paraphrase: all the world's creation is jhooth; understand this, O friend. Then: says Nanak, it does not stay steady, like a wall of sand. Jhooth is usually translated false. But look at how the salok explains itself. It doesn't say the world is a trick. It says thir naa rahai: it doesn't stay put. And it gives the picture: baaloo kee bheet, a wall of sand. A sand wall isn't a lie. It's really there. You can touch it, lean on it for a moment. It just won't hold. That's the sense of jhooth here: not fake, but not lasting. Something you can't build your whole weight on. Remember rachnaa, too. On day five hundred eighty-one we heard rachnaa raam banaaee, the creation the Lord made. Same word. The creation is His. What's jhooth is the idea that it will stand forever. And listen to the tone: re meet, O friend. The Guru isn't lecturing a sinner. He's talking to a friend, the way you'd gently tell someone you love not to lean a ladder against loose sand. So today's line, hold it lightly, isn't a call to despise anything. Enjoy the house. Love the people. Do the work well. Just don't lean your whole life against a wall that's already slipping at the top. Lean on what stays, the Name we heard about yesterday. Six hundred days in, that's worth hearing: everything here is lent, and the lender is the One who stays.
screen: `JAG RACHNAA SABH JHOOTH HAI.` · `THIR NAA RAHAI: IT DOESN'T STAY.` · `BAALOO KEE BHEET: A WALL OF SAND.` · `RE MEET: SAID TO A FRIEND.` · then, large: `HOLD IT LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one attachment. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of one thing you've been leaning on with your whole weight: a plan, a status, an outcome you've decided must happen, someone's approval. Picture it as a wall of sand you're pressed against. Now, gently, take one step back. You don't have to knock it down. Just stand on your own feet, near it, not against it. Feel the ground under you. If you pray, you can lean on Waheguru instead, for these breaths. The bell holds the time.
Jhooth. The salok calls the world's creation jhooth, not because it's fake, but because, like a wall of sand, it doesn't stay steady, and it says so as one friend to another.
Your line: hold it lightly. Today, with one thing you care about, enjoy it fully and lean on it a little less. Day six hundred.

howItsDone: This salok is among the ninth Guru's saloks read at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh teachers explain its jhooth as 'not lasting' rather than 'fake', pointing to its image of a wall of sand.

fork.setup: the salok calls the world jhooth. what picture does it give to explain?
options: a wall of sand that doesn't stay steady.
a painting of a fake landscape.
fork.reveal: says Nanak, it does not stay steady, like a wall of sand. jhooth here means not lasting, not fake.

original.note: Gurmukhi: jhooth, usually 'false'; in this salok, what doesn't last, like a wall of sand.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world's creation is false means nothing is real.
what it means: the world is real but not lasting; hold it lightly and lean on what stays.
what a scholar hears: Gurbani often sets jhooth against sach, the true, which also means the eternal, so jhooth carries the sense of the passing, not merely the untrue.
